paper_a.title: A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems

paper_b.title: A Tutorial on Hidden Markov Models and Selected Applications in Speech Recognition

metadata.description: Both papers develop recursive Bayesian state-space inference. Kalman (paper373) handles linear-Gaussian continuous-state systems, deriving the filter from orthogonal projection on the observation manifold; Rabiner (paper375) handles discrete-state HMMs via the forward-backward / Viterbi / Baum-Welch trinity. The two share the same recursive predict-update filtering machinery applied to state-space models, but operate on different state spaces (continuous-Gaussian vs discrete) and serve different objectives (MMSE estimation vs likelihood evaluation, MAP decoding, and ML training). Both are PDF-fallback extractions; node-level alignment was made via name + type with reduced LaTeX fidelity.

matches.explanation: Kalman's state-space model x(t+1) = Phi x(t) + u(t) with output y(t) = M(t) x(t) is the linear-Gaussian continuous-state analogue of the HMM specification (Markov chain DP375.1 + hidden state with state-dependent emissions DP375.2 + parameter set lambda=(A,B,pi) DP375.3). Both rely on the same first-order Markov state evolution and conditional output independence (AssumP375.1). The forms differ (linear matrix recursion plus Gaussian noise vs. categorical transition/emission matrices), but the modeling role is identical.

Kalman's notion of 'state' as the minimal sufficient statistic for predicting the future generalises the discrete Markov-chain state in HMMs. Rabiner's first-order Markov chain (DP375.1) is the discrete instance of the same concept: the state captures everything from the past that matters for the future.

Kalman's continuous-time linear dynamic system (DP373.9) and discrete-time transition matrix Phi (DP373.10) play the same role as the HMM transition matrix A = {a_ij} (inside DP375.1): they encode the state-evolution rule. The Kalman version is a deterministic linear map in R^n; the HMM version is a stochastic matrix on a finite alphabet.

Kalman's orthogonal projection x_bar(t1|t) = E_hat[x(t1)|Y(t)] (DP373.7, DP373.13) is the conditional state estimate given observations. Its HMM analogue is the state posterior gamma_t(i) = P(q_t = S_i | O, lambda) (DP375.6). In the Gaussian case the projection equals the conditional mean; in the discrete-state HMM the posterior is a categorical distribution. Both are 'filtered/smoothed state estimates' — same conceptual role, different state space.

Kalman's innovation y_tilde(t|t-1) = y(t) - M(t) x*(t|t-1) — the part of the new observation orthogonal to the past — is conceptually paralleled by the HMM forward/backward variables alpha_t(i) and beta_t(i), which propagate the past/future observation information up to a state. The match is rough: innovations decompose y(t) into 'predicted' and 'new', while alpha/beta accumulate likelihood prefixes/suffixes; both are the 'message-passing' quantities of recursive filtering.

The L2-geometric machinery (linear manifold Y(t), orthogonality, orthonormal basis) is intrinsic to Kalman's projection-based derivation but has no direct counterpart in the discrete-state HMM tutorial, where probabilistic message-passing is used instead.

Kalman's Wiener problem (estimate x_1(t_1) from noisy y observations on [t_0, t]) covers filtering, prediction and smoothing. Its HMM counterpart splits into two of Rabiner's three fundamental problems: Problem 1 (evaluation, computing P(O|lambda)) and Problem 2 (decoding the best state sequence). Both are 'inference given a state-space model'; the answers differ (continuous MMSE estimate of state vs. likelihood + most likely state path).

Sherman / Doob result that the conditional expectation minimises symmetric / quadratic loss is foundational to Kalman but is never invoked in Rabiner's tutorial — HMM decoding uses MAP/Viterbi, and HMM training uses ML, not MMSE.
Theorem 2 (optimal estimate equals orthogonal projection in the Gaussian / linear-MSE case) is paper-original to Kalman's geometric derivation and has no corresponding theorem in the HMM tutorial.

This is the central methodological alignment of the pair. Kalman's Theorem 3 / Algorithm AP373.1 — the recursive prediction-update filter with gain Delta*(t), closed-loop transition Phi*(t+1;t), and covariance recursion P*(t+1) — is the linear-Gaussian continuous-state analogue of HMM's forward (AP375.1) and backward (AP375.2) algorithms with their recursions EP375.1 and EP375.2. Both are O(N^2 T) (or matrix-recursive) trellis-like procedures that propagate sufficient statistics through time given a state-space model. The mathematics is different (matrix Riccati update vs. categorical alpha/beta updates), but the recursive predict-update structure is shared. PP373.3 (induction-based projection-onto-innovation derivation) plays the same role as the inductive forward-recursion derivation.

Step-level alignment of the two recursive filters: initialise (Kalman ASP373.1: x*=0, P*=Ex(t_0)x'(t_0); HMM ASP375.1: alpha_1(i)=pi_i b_i(O_1)), recurse (ASP373.2 predict-update gain/transition/state/covariance loop; ASP375.2 alpha_{t+1}(j) induction), and termination/output (ASP373.3 multistep prediction; ASP375.3 P(O|lambda)=sum alpha_T(i)). Emitted as a single composite L2-vs-L2 entry tied to the parent algorithm match above.

The matrix Riccati covariance equation (Wiener-Hopf analogue in Kalman's framework) is paper-original Kalman content with no counterpart in the discrete-emission HMM tutorial — HMMs do not propagate a state covariance because the state posterior is a categorical distribution, not a Gaussian.

Kalman's remark that the innovation is white noise (the post-summer feedback signal of the optimal filter) is a structural observation specific to linear-Gaussian filtering. Loosely, it parallels the role of HMM forward/backward variables as the 'sufficient information channel' through the state-space, but the parallel is structural rather than mathematical.
Continuous-time-limit recovery of an ODE filter is specific to Kalman's continuous setting; HMMs are intrinsically discrete-time.

Both note handling of finite/non-stationary data: Kalman's RP373.3 emphasises that nonstationarity and growing memory pose no obstacle to his recursions, paralleling Rabiner's multi-sequence reestimation (AP375.6) which trains over multiple finite sequences. Weak conceptual match.

Kalman's dual problem (LQR-type optimal control regulator) and the duality theorem between filtering and control have no analogue in the HMM tutorial — Rabiner does not develop a control-theoretic dual.

Pedagogical worked examples in each paper. Kalman's scalar signal-plus-white-noise (ExP373.1) and position-velocity tracking (ExP373.2) play the role that Rabiner's weather-Markov-chain (ExP375.1), coin-toss models (ExP375.2) and urn-and-ball model (ExP375.3) play for HMMs: small concrete instances. Same conceptual role; very different examples.

Viterbi best-path decoding (delta_t(i) score, dynamic-programming algorithm AP375.3, and recursion EP375.3) is paper-B-original (cited from Viterbi 1967 / Forney 1973). It is the discrete-state analogue of MAP path estimation and has no counterpart in Kalman's MMSE-only treatment.

The two-state transition posterior xi_t(i,j) is HMM-specific (used in Baum-Welch). Kalman's continuous-state recursion has no analogue: transitions are deterministic linear maps and one-step posteriors are joint Gaussian moments, not categorical.

HMM topology choices (ergodic, left-right Bakis, null transitions) are paper-B-original modeling decisions on the discrete-state graph. Kalman's continuous linear system has no analogous topology question.

Continuous-density and autoregressive HMM emission models (Gaussian mixtures, AR processes per state) are HMM-extensions specific to Rabiner. Kalman's emission y(t) = M(t) x(t) is already linear-Gaussian and does not require these elaborations.

Explicit-duration HMMs and the geometric duration density of standard HMMs are duration-modeling refinements particular to discrete state chains. Kalman has no direct counterpart since his continuous-state model implicitly handles 'duration' through linear dynamics.
Parameter tying and deleted interpolation are sparse-data smoothing techniques for HMM training; Kalman's paper does not address parameter learning.
Model distance between two HMMs and the identifiability-of-HMMs proposition are HMM-specific theoretical content with no Kalman counterpart.
VQ codebook is a speech-preprocessing concept used to discretise continuous features for use with discrete-emission HMMs; it is far outside Kalman's scope.
Problem 3 (parameter estimation by ML) is HMM-original. Kalman 1960 assumes the state-space matrices Phi, M, Q are given — there is no parameter-learning problem in his paper.
Speech-recognition application problems (isolated and connected word recognition) are application-specific to Rabiner; Kalman 1960 has no application-domain problem.

The Baum-Welch / EM training apparatus for HMMs (algorithm, reestimation formulas, monotone-likelihood theorem, auxiliary-Q-function, equivalence-with-EM, Lagrange critical-point form, and proof) is the entire model-learning pillar that is absent from Kalman 1960. This is the largest paper-B-only block.

Scaled forward-backward and the log-likelihood-from-scale-factors equation are numerical-stability tricks specific to long-sequence HMM computations; Kalman's matrix recursion has its own conditioning concerns but no direct analogue here.
Segmental K-means training and level-building connected-word recognition are speech-engineering pipelines particular to Rabiner.
